title: The Monk Who Invented Anesthesia
event_summary: The physician Hua Tuo developed mafeisan (麻沸散), a powdered oral anesthetic compound likely combining datura, aconitum, and cannabis, enabling him to perform abdominal surgeries, organ resections, and even partial splenectomies on fully unconscious patients in second-century China. He reportedly performed the first recorded use of general anesthesia for major surgery, predating Western anesthesia by over 1,600 years. His techniques were documented by contemporaries, and he became legendary for painless operations that included intestinal anastomosis—reconnecting severed bowels.
why_forgotten: Hua Tuo was executed on the orders of warlord Cao Cao around 208 AD, and according to the Records of the Three Kingdoms, he burned or his jailer destroyed his medical manuscripts before death, erasing the exact formula of mafeisan permanently. Subsequent Chinese medical tradition shifted toward acupuncture and herbal internal medicine, and invasive surgery fell into cultural disfavor for centuries. Western medical history long dismissed the accounts as legend, unwilling to credit pre-modern China with a breakthrough Europeans didn't achieve until the 1840s.
why_it_matters: Hua Tuo's lost anesthetic demonstrates that the concept of rendering patients unconscious for surgery was achievable with plant-based compounds long before ether and chloroform, and modern ethnobotanists have reconstructed plausible mafeisan formulas using the plants he likely employed. His story reshaped debates about why general anesthesia took so long to re-emerge, suggesting cultural and political factors—not technical impossibility—delayed one of medicine's most essential innovations. Today, researchers studying traditional Chinese pharmacopeia cite his work as evidence that plant-derived anesthetics deserve renewed scientific investigation.
